The reproductive biology of Archaster typicus was investigated under controlled aquarium conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. Females produced eggs with a diameter of 0.15 millimeters, which subsequent volumetric calculations indicated would yield a wet weight at birth of approximately 1.7 micrograms [Wwb = approximately 1.7 micrograms]. This remarkably low neonatal mass reflects the planktotrophic larval strategy characteristic of many tropical asteroids, wherein a tiny, free-swimming bipinnaria larva must feed externally before undergoing metamorphosis. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), calculated as the ratio of gonad mass to total body mass, reached 10% [GSI = 10%] at 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C] during the peak spawning period.

Larval development was monitored through the bipinnaria and subsequent metamorphic stages in the laboratory. After fertilization and the formation of free-swimming, planktotrophic larvae, metamorphic competence and settlement onto the substratum were observed after approximately 30 days  under the prevailing thermal regime of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. This duration of planktonic life is comparable to that reported for other congeneric species inhabiting warm Indo-Pacific waters, where elevated temperatures accelerate developmental rates. The transition from a bilateral, ciliated larval form to a pentaradial, benthic juvenile represents a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, as successful recruitment depends on the availability of suitable sandy habitats and adequate microbial film cues for triggering the settlement response. The newly settled starfish, already possessing a functional madreporite, then commence a period of rapid somatic growth.

Juvenile growth trajectories and the timing of sexual maturation were assessed from a cohort reared in flow-through seawater systems. The onset of puberty, defined by the first observation of gonadal differentiation and gametogenesis, occurred at 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] at the experimental temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. At this stage, individuals had attained a radius length of approximately 29 millimeters, corresponding to a wet body weight at puberty calculated as 3.16 grams [Wwp = 3.16 grams]. This allometric relationship between radius and mass is typical for growing asteroids and indicates that a minimum body size threshold must be reached before energy is diverted from somatic maintenance and growth into the development of reproductive structures. The delay of nearly one year before the onset of reproductive maturity implies a relatively slow life history compared to some smaller, more rapidly maturing tropical echinoderms.

The maximum individual lifespan, derived from field recapture studies and supplemented by captive observations, was estimated at approximately 17 years [am = approximately 17 years] in animals maintained at 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. This longevity, exceeding seventeen years, positions Archaster typicus among the longer-lived members of the family Astropectinidae and suggests a life-history strategy that emphasizes repeated reproductive bouts and extended somatic persistence over a single, high-investment spawning event. The ultimate wet weight recorded for the largest, reproductively senescent adults in the population reached 28.6 grams [Wwi = 28.6 grams], a figure that represents the maximum asymptotic body mass attainable under favourable feeding conditions. This plateau in mass gain likely reflects the energetic limits imposed by the animal's foraging mode as a deposit feeder on intertidal and shallow subtidal sandy flats.

Comparative analyses across tropical asteroid taxa reveal that the life-history parameters of Archaster typicus are finely tuned to the stable, warm thermal environment it inhabits. The time elapsed from birth to the pubertal stage, measured as 365 days [tp = 365 days] at the ambient seawater temperature of approximately 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C], allows juveniles a full year of growth to reach a size refuge from some predators. The gonadosomatic index was 10% [GSI = 10%] at a temperature of 29.5 °C [T = 29.5 °C]. The wet weight at birth of just approximately 1.7 micrograms [Wwb = approximately 1.7 micrograms] underscores the high fecundity needed to offset larval mortality. These integrated traits depict a species that balances modest per-event reproductive investment with an exceptionally protracted adult lifespan, a combination well suited to the relatively predictable, low-stress conditions of its tropical sand-flat habitat.
